# Repeated Measures ANOVA

## Repeated Measures ANOVA

It is sometimes the case that we have *repeated measures* data

::: subpoint
○ Responses collected on the same measure for the same subjects more than one time
:::

Some examples of repeated measures data are...

::: subpoint
○ A mental health screening questionnaire given to participants once per day
:::

::: subpoint
○ A yearly customer satisfaction survey
:::

For these designs, we have to consider if conditions are **between-person** or **within-person**.


## Repeated Measures Model


## Repeated Measures Example

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="85%"}
Remember the chick dataset from Lab 06?

We are going to use... another chick dataset!

Instead of having one value of chick weight for each chick, this one tracks chicks over time. We will have weekly updates on each chick's weight.
:::

::: {.column width="15%"}
![](https://mannapro.com/cdn/shop/articles/how-to-raise-baby-chickens_2x_b6a71ebc-2d08-4bdc-82b0-18ccf861c9bd.jpg?v=1740003489)
:::
::::


## Repeated Measures Example

```{r}
chick_data <- read_csv(here::here("lab", "data", "lab_11", "chick_week_data.csv"))
chick_data
```


## Repeated Measures Example

```{r}
# install.packages("psych")
psych::describe(chick_data)
```

## Repeated Measures Example

We want to estimate the effect of week of the experiment on chick weight! Is `week` a between- or within-subject (chick) factor? [Within!]{.fragment} [What about diet?]{.fragment} [Between!]{.fragment}

::: fragment
Can see in the data that within every chick (`.by = chick`), there are four levels of week (`n_distinct(week)`) but only one level of diet (`n_distinct(diet)`).

```{r}
chick_data |>
  summarize(
    .by = chick,
    n_diets = n_distinct(diet),
    n_weeks = n_distinct(week)
  )
```
:::


## Repeated Measures Example

```{r}
chick_data |> head(4)
```

Notice that all the variables in this dataset are `double`s (decimal point numbers). The ANOVA functions want to treat these as `factor`s.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
chick_cleaned <- chick_data |>
  mutate(chick = factor(chick),
         week = factor(week),
         diet = factor(diet))
```

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
chick_cleaned <- chick_data |>
  mutate(
    across(c(chick, week, diet), factor)
  )
```
:::
::::





## Aside: `across()`

`across()` is a helpful `{tidyverse}` function that can be used within functions like `summarize()` and `mutate()`.

When we want to apply the same transformation to multiple columns, we can target them all with `across()` and specify the transformation once, instead of manually specifying each one.

`across(columns, function(s))`

::: subpoint
○ `columns` = `<tidy-select>` columns to target
:::

::: subpoint
○ `function(s)` = name of function to use, *anonymous function*, or list of functions.
:::


## Aside: `across()`

Examples of `across()`...


::: {.panel-tabset}
### Name of Function

Just like we did before

```{r}
chick_data |>
  mutate(across(c(chick, week, diet), factor))
```

### Anonymous Function

::: {style="font-size:90%"}
Example of standardizing across all columns (not necessarily helpful here). Reminder: within `function()`, `column` just serves as a placeholder name for that column. You can name this whatever you want, as long as you use the same name within the actual function part.
:::

```{r}
chick_data |>
  mutate(across(everything(), function(column) (column - mean(column)) / sd(column)))
```

### List of Functions

Example of summarizing columns by multiple functions

```{r}
chick_data |>
  summarize(across(
      where(is.numeric), 
      list(min = min, 
           max = max, 
           mean = function(column) mean(column, na.rm = T))
    ))
```
:::


## Aside: `across()`

Our original `across()` method successfully converted the intended columns to `factor()`s.

```{r}
chick_cleaned <- chick_data |>
  mutate(
    across(c(chick, week, diet), factor)
  )

chick_cleaned
```


## Repeated Measures Example

`ez::ezANOVA(data, dv, wid, within = NULL, between = NULL, type = 2)`

::: subpoint
○ `dv` = the outcome variable
:::

::: subpoint
○ `wid` = name of the column with subject identifier. Typically contains an `id` for each person (here, each chick!)
:::

::: subpoint
○ `within` = column(s) with within-subject factors
:::

::: subpoint
○ `between` = column(s) with between-subject factors
:::

::: subpoint
○ `type` = the sums of squares method used
:::

`= NULL` means the default is set to `NULL`, and you do not necessarily need to input a value for that argument for the function to work. (May need to specify it for the function to work the way you *want*, though! Depends on your ANOVA goal.)


## Balanced or Unbalanced

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
chick_cleaned |> 
  count(week)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
What type of Sums of Squares should we use?

[Doesn't matter!]{.fragment}
:::
::::


## Repeated Measures Example

`ez::ezANOVA(data, dv, wid, within = NULL, between = NULL, type = 2)`

```{r}
chick_weight_model <- ez::ezANOVA(
  data = chick_cleaned,
  dv = weight,
  wid = chick,
  within = week
)
chick_weight_model
```


## Assumptions

```{r}
chick_cleaned |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = week, 
              names_prefix = "week_", 
              values_from = weight) |>
  select(starts_with("week")) |>
  cov()
```

**Sphericity**: are the elements on the diagonal all equal in the population?

**Compound Symmetry**: are the elements on the diagonal AND on the off-diagonals all equal in the population?


## Assumptions

If assumption holds, `W` should be close to 1 and `p` will be large ($p > .05$).

```{r}
chick_weight_model$`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity`
```


## Assumptions Corrections

```{r}
chick_weight_model$`Sphericity Corrections`
```


## Results

```{r}
chick_weight_model
```

We observe a significant effect of week on chick weight.


## Estimated Marginal Means

```{r}
#| error: true
emmeans::emmeans(chick_weight_model)
```

`ezANOVA()` returns dataframes, and `emmeans()` isn't able to turn those into EMMS. You'd have to refit with `return_aov = T` and also make sure the contrasts have been set to orthogonal before (even if it is a balanced design!).

```{r}
options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))

chick_weight_model <- ez::ezANOVA(
  data = chick_cleaned,
  dv = weight,
  wid = chick,
  within = week,
  return_aov = T
)
chick_weight_model$aov |> emmeans::emmeans("week")
```

That's an annoying extra step to deal with...


## Resetting

```{r}
options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))
```


## `afex` ANOVAs

Unfortunately, the `{ez}` package is not being maintained very much right now, so it is less equipped to integrate with other tools like `{emmeans}`. Another package with ANOVA functionality, `{afex}`, is! It has many ways of specifying the form of the ANOVA you want to estimate, including one very similar to the `ezANOVA()` syntax.

`afex::aov_ez(id, dv, data, between = NULL, within = NULL, type = 3)`

::: subpoint
○ `id` = **character vector** name of the column with subject identifier
:::

::: subpoint
○ `dv` = **character vector** the outcome variable
:::

::: subpoint
○ `within` = **character vector** column(s) with within-subject factors
:::

::: subpoint
○ `between` = **character vector** column(s) with between-subject factors
:::

::: subpoint
○ `type` = the sums of squares method used
:::

Note that `afex::aov_ez()` uses Type III sums of squares by default.



## `afex` ANOVAs

Unfortunately, the `{ez}` package is not being maintained very much right now, so it is less equipped to integrate with other tools like `{emmeans}`. Another package with ANOVA functionality, `{afex}`, is! It has many ways of specifying the form of the ANOVA you want to estimate, including one very similar to the `ezANOVA()` syntax.

`afex::aov_ez(id, dv, data, between = NULL, within = NULL, type = 3)`

```{r}
chick_weight_model_afex <- afex::aov_ez(
  data = chick_cleaned,
  dv = "weight",
  id = "chick",
  within = "week"
)
summary(chick_weight_model_afex)
```


## Estimated Marginal Means

```{r}
emms_week <- emmeans::emmeans(chick_weight_model_afex, specs = "week")
emms_week
```

Note than `emmeans()` slightly adjusted the labeling of the week value. We can prevent that by going back to data cleaning and not letting the levels within that variable start with a number.


## Estimated Marginal Means

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
chick_cleaned <- chick_data |>
  mutate(
    across(c(chick, week, diet), factor),
    week = paste0("week_", week)
  )
chick_cleaned
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
chick_weight_model_afex <- afex::aov_ez(
  data = chick_cleaned,
  dv = "weight",
  id = "chick",
  within = "week"
)
emms_week <- emmeans::emmeans(chick_weight_model_afex, specs = "week")
emms_week
```
:::
::::


## Visualization

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
# install.packages("ggdist")

emms_week |>
  as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = emmean, ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL)) +
  ggdist::geom_dots(
    data = chick_cleaned, 
    aes(x = week, y = weight), 
    inherit.aes = F,
    alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_linerange() +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = parse_number) + # applying the `parse_number()` function to the labels
  labs(y = "Weight", x = "Week",
       caption = "Line ranges represent 95% confidence intervals. Gray points represent observed data.") +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T)) +
  theme_classic()
```

# Mixed ANOVA

## Mixed ANOVA

We aren't just limited to between- **OR** within-subject factors, can also test combinations of both.


## Mixed ANOVA Example

We can also consider the effect of diet given to the chicks on their weight!

```{r}
chick_weight_diet_model <- afex::aov_ez(
  data = chick_cleaned,
  dv = "weight",
  id = "chick",
  within = "week",
  between = "diet"
)
summary(chick_weight_diet_model)
```


## Balanced or Unbalanced

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
chick_cleaned |> 
  count(week, diet) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = diet, names_prefix = "week_", values_from = n)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
What type of Sums of Squares should we use?

[Do we think an interaction between week and diet would be negligible?]{.fragment} [Maybe not! Let's do Type III]{.fragment}

[`afex` does Type III sums of squares by default... and also automatically changes the contrasts to `contr.sum`!]{.fragment}
:::
::::


## Mixed ANOVA Example

We can also consider the effect of diet given to the chicks on their weight!

```{r}
options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))
chick_weight_diet_model_ez <- ez::ezANOVA(
  data = chick_cleaned,
  dv = weight,
  wid = chick,
  within = week,
  between = diet,
  type = 3
)
chick_weight_diet_model
```


## Visualization

```{r}
emms_week_diet <- emmeans::emmeans(chick_weight_diet_model, specs = c("diet", "week"))
emms_week_diet
```

# Multilevel Modeling

## Multilevel Modeling

Multilevel Modeling (MLM) is a more flexible framework for examining between- and within-subject variation!

ANOVA can't handle missing cells (e.g., if we were missing weight observations for diet 3 in week 4), but MLM can! It can also handle uneven spaces between time intervals (e.g., if we had observations on day 1, day 5, day 6, day 8, and day 30).



## Multilevel Modeling Example

Just within factor...

```{r}
# install.packages("lme4")
chick_weight_model_lmer <- lme4::lmer(weight ~ 1 + week + (1 | chick), data = chick_cleaned)
summary(chick_weight_model_lmer)
```


## Multilevel Modeling Example

Within and between factor...

```{r}
# install.packages("lme4")
chick_weight_diet_model_lmer <- lme4::lmer(weight ~ week * diet + (1 | chick), data = chick_cleaned)
summary(chick_weight_diet_model_lmer)
```


## Bayesian Multilevel Modeling


```{r}
#| eval: false
library(rstanarm)
chick_weight_diet_model_bayes <- stan_lmer(
  weight ~ week * diet + (1 | chick), 
  data = chick_cleaned
)

summary(chick_weight_diet_model_bayes)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(rstanarm)
chick_weight_diet_model_bayes <- stan_lmer(
  weight ~ week * diet + (1 | chick), 
  data = chick_cleaned,
  refresh = 0
)
summary(chick_weight_diet_model_bayes)
```



## Bayesian Multilevel Modeling

```{r}
summary(chick_weight_diet_model_bayes, pars = c("alpha", "beta", "sigma", "Sigma[chick:(Intercept),(Intercept)]"))
```


## Diagnostics

```{r}
#| fig-width: 18
#| fig-height: 8
pars_for_trace_plot <- c(
  names(fixef(chick_weight_diet_model_bayes)),
  "sigma",
  "Sigma[chick:(Intercept),(Intercept)]"
)

bayesplot::mcmc_trace(chick_weight_diet_model_bayes, pars = pars_for_trace_plot, facet_args = list(ncol = 6))
```


## Estimated Marginal Means

```{r}
emms_bayes <- emmeans::emmeans(chick_weight_diet_model_bayes, specs = c("diet", "week"))
emms_bayes
```
